text: Bayesian Deep Ensembles via the Neural Tangent Kernel

We explore the link between deep ensembles and Gaussian processes (GPs) through the lens of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK): a recent development in understanding the training dynamics of wide neural networks (NNs). Previous work has shown that even in the infinite width limit, when NNs become GPs, there is no GP posterior interpretation to a deep ensemble trained with squared error loss. We introduce a simple modification to standard deep ensembles training, through addition of a computationally-tractable, randomised and untrainable function to each ensemble member, that enables a posterior interpretation in the infinite width limit. When ensembled together, our trained NNs give an approximation to a posterior predictive distribution, and we prove that our Bayesian deep ensembles make more conservative predictions than standard deep ensembles in the infinite width limit. Finally, using finite width NNs we demonstrate that our Bayesian deep ensembles faithfully emulate the analytic posterior predictive when available, and can outperform standard deep ensembles in various out-of-distribution settings, for both regression and classification tasks.
1 Introduction

Consider a training dataset [MATH \mathcal{D}] consisting of [MATH N] i.i.d. data points [MATH \mathcal{D}=\{\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}\}=\{({\bm{x}}_{n},y_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N}] , with [MATH {\bm{x}}\mkern 1.5mu{\in}\mkern 1.5mu\mathbb{R}^{d}] representing [MATH d] -dimensional features and [MATH y] representing [MATH C] -dimensional targets. Given input features [MATH {\bm{x}}] and parameters [MATH {\bm{\theta}}\mkern 1.5mu{\in}\mkern 1.5mu\mathbb{R}^{p}] we use the output, [MATH f({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}})\mkern 1.5mu{\in}\mkern 1.5mu\mathbb{R}^{C}] , of a neural network (NN) to model the predictive distribution [MATH p(y|{\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}})] over the targets. For univariate regression tasks, [MATH p(y|{\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}})] will be Gaussian: [MATH -\textrm{log}\hskip 1.42262ptp(y|{\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}})] is the squared error [MATH \frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(y-f({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}))^{2}] up to additive constant, for fixed observation noise [MATH \sigma^{2}\mkern 1.5mu{\in}\mkern 1.5mu\mathbb{R}_{+}] . For classification tasks, [MATH p(y|{\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}})] will be a Categorical distribution.

Given a prior distribution [MATH p({\bm{\theta}})] over the parameters, we can define the posterior over [MATH {\bm{\theta}}] , [MATH p({\bm{\theta}}|\mathcal{D})] , using Bayes’ rule and subsequently the posterior predictive distribution at a test point [MATH ({\bm{x}}^{*},y^{*})] :
[MATH \displaystyle p(y^{*}|{\bm{x}}^{*},\mathcal{D})=\int p(y^{*}|{\bm{x}}^{*},{\bm{\theta}})p({\bm{\theta}}|\mathcal{D})\,d{\bm{\theta}}] (1)

The posterior predictive is appealing as it represents a marginalisation over [MATH {\bm{\theta}}] weighted by posterior probabilities, and has been shown to be optimal for minimising predictive risk under a well-specified model [ 1 ] . However, one issue with the posterior predictive for NNs is that it is computationally intensive to calculate the posterior [MATH p({\bm{\theta}}|\mathcal{D})] exactly. Several approximations to [MATH p({\bm{\theta}}|\mathcal{D})] have been introduced for Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) including: Laplace approximation [ 2 ] ; Markov chain Monte Carlo [ 3 , 4 ] ; variational inference [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] ; and Monte-Carlo dropout [ 10 ] .

Despite the recent interest in BNNs, it has been shown empirically that deep ensembles [ 11 ] , which lack a principled Bayesian justification, outperform existing BNNs in terms of uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution robustness, cf. [ 12 ] . Deep ensembles independently initialise and train individual NNs (referred to herein as baselearners ) on the negative log-likelihood loss [MATH \mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}})\mkern 1.5mu{=}\mkern 1.5mu\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell(y_{n},f({\bm{x}}_{n},{\bm{\theta}}))] with [MATH \ell(y,f({\bm{x}},{{\bm{\theta}}}))\mkern 1.5mu{=}\mkern 1.5mu\mkern 1.5mu{-}\mkern 1.5mu\textrm{log}\hskip 1.42262ptp(y|{\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}})] , before aggregating predictions. Understanding the success of deep ensembles, particularly in relation to Bayesian inference, is a key question in the uncertainty quantification and Bayesian deep learning communities at present: Fort et al. [13] suggested that the empirical performance of deep ensembles is explained by their ability to explore different functional modes, while Wilson and Izmailov [14] argued that deep ensembles are actually approximating the posterior predictive.

In this work, we will relate deep ensembles to Bayesian inference, using recent developments connecting GPs and wide NNs, both before [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] and after [ 22 , 23 ] training. Using these insights, we devise a modification to standard NN training that yields an exact posterior sample for [MATH f(\cdot,{\bm{\theta}})] in the infinite width limit. As a result, when ensembled together our modified baselearners give a posterior predictive approximation, and can thus be viewed as a Bayesian deep ensemble .

One concept that is related to our methods concerns ensembles trained with Randomised Priors to give an approximate posterior interpretation, which we will use when modelling observation noise in regression tasks. The idea behind randomised priors is that, under certain conditions, regularising baselearner NNs towards independently drawn “priors” during training produces exact posterior samples for [MATH f(\cdot,{\bm{\theta}})] . Randomised priors recently appeared in machine learning applied to reinforcement learning [ 24 ] and uncertainty quantification [ 25 , 26 ] , like this work. To the best of our knowledge, related ideas first appeared in astrophysics where they were applied to Gaussian random fields [ 27 ] . However, one such condition for posterior exactness with randomised priors is that the model [MATH f({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}})] is linear in [MATH {\bm{\theta}}] . This is not true in general for NNs, but has been shown to hold for wide NNs local to their parameter initialisation, in a recent line of work. In order to introduce our methods, we will first review this line of work, known as the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) [ 22 ] .
2 NTK Background
Wide NNs, and their relation to GPs, have been a fruitful area recently for the theoretical study of NNs: we review only the most salient developments to this work, due to limited space.
First introduced by Jacot et al. [22] , the empirical NTK of [MATH f(\cdot,{\bm{\theta}}_{t})] is, for inputs [MATH {\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime}] , the kernel:
[MATH \displaystyle\hat{\Theta}_{t}({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime})=\langle\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}f({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}_{t}),\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}f({\bm{x}}^{\prime},{\bm{\theta}}_{t})\rangle] (2)

and describes the functional gradient of a NN in terms of the current loss incurred on the training set. Note that [MATH {\bm{\theta}}_{t}] depends on a random initialisation [MATH {\bm{\theta}}_{0}] , thus the empirical NTK is random for all [MATH t>0] .

Jacot et al. [22] showed that for an MLP under a so-called NTK parameterisation, detailed in Appendix A , the empirical NTK converges in probability to a deterministic limit [MATH \Theta] , that stays constant during gradient training, as the hidden layer widths of the NN go to infinity sequentially. Later, Yang [28] , Yang [29] extended the NTK convergence result to convergence almost surely, which is proven rigorously for a variety of architectures and for widths (or channels in Convolutional NNs) of hidden layers going to infinity in unison. This limiting positive-definite (p.d.) kernel [MATH \Theta] , known as the NTK, depends only on certain NN architecture choices, including: activation, depth and variances for weight and bias parameters. Note that the NTK parameterisation can be thought of as akin to training under standard parameterisation with a learning rate that is inversely proportional to the width of the NN, which has been shown to be the largest scale for stable learning rates in wide NNs [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] .

Lee et al. [23] built on the results of Jacot et al. [22] , and studied the linearised regime of an NN. Specifically, if we denote as [MATH f_{t}({\bm{x}})=f({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}_{t})] the network function at time [MATH t] , we can define the first order Taylor expansion of the network function around randomly initialised parameters [MATH {\bm{\theta}}_{0}] to be:
[MATH \displaystyle f_{t}^{\text{lin}}({\bm{x}})=f_{0}({\bm{x}})+\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}f({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}_{0})\Delta{\bm{\theta}}_{t}] (3)
where [MATH \Delta{\bm{\theta}}_{t}={\bm{\theta}}_{t}-{\bm{\theta}}_{0}] and [MATH f_{0}=f(\cdot,{\bm{\theta}}_{0})] is the randomly initialised NN function.

For notational clarity, whenever we evaluate a function at an arbitrary input set [MATH \mathcal{X}^{\prime}] instead of a single point [MATH {\bm{x}}^{\prime}] , we suppose the function is vectorised. For example, [MATH f_{t}(\mathcal{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{NC}] denotes the concatenated NN outputs on training set [MATH \mathcal{X}] , whereas [MATH \nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}f_{t}(\mathcal{X})=\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}f(\mathcal{X},{\bm{\theta}}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{NC\times p}] . In the interest of space, we will also sometimes use subscripts to signify kernel inputs, so for instance [MATH \Theta_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\mathcal{X}}^{\mathstrut}=\Theta({\bm{x}}^{\prime},\mathcal{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times NC}] and [MATH \Theta_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{X}}^{\mathstrut}=\Theta(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{NC\times NC}] throughout this work.

The results of Lee et al. [23] showed that in the infinite width limit, with NTK parameterisation and gradient flow under squared error loss, [MATH f_{t}^{\text{lin}}({\bm{x}})] and [MATH f_{t}({\bm{x}})] are equal for any [MATH t\geq 0] , for a shared random initialisation [MATH {\bm{\theta}}_{0}] . In particular, for the linearised network it can be shown, that as [MATH t{\rightarrow}\infty] :
[MATH \displaystyle f_{\infty}^{\text{lin}}({\bm{x}})=f_{0}({\bm{x}})-\hat{\Theta}_{0}({\bm{x}},\mathcal{X})\hat{\Theta}_{0}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{X})^{-1}(f_{0}(\mathcal{X})-\mathcal{Y})] (4)
and thus as the hidden layer widths converge to infinity we have that:
[MATH \displaystyle f_{\infty}^{\text{lin}}({\bm{x}})=f_{\infty}({\bm{x}})=f_{0}({\bm{x}})-\Theta({\bm{x}},\mathcal{X})\Theta(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{X})^{-1}(f_{0}(\mathcal{X})-\mathcal{Y})] (5)

We can replace [MATH \Theta(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{X})^{-1}] with the generalised inverse when invertibility is an issue. However, this will not be a main concern of this work, as our methods will add regularisation that corresponds to modelling observation/output noise, which both ensures invertibility and alleviates any potential convergence issues due to fast decay of the NTK eigenspectrum [ 33 ] .

From Eq. ( 5 ) we see that, conditional on the training data [MATH \{\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}\}] , we can decompose [MATH f_{\infty}] into [MATH f_{\infty}({\bm{x}})=\mu({\bm{x}})\mkern 1.5mu{+}\mkern 1.5mu\gamma({\bm{x}})] where [MATH \mu({\bm{x}})=\Theta({\bm{x}},\mathcal{X})\Theta(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{X})^{-1}\mathcal{Y}] is a deterministic mean and [MATH \gamma({\bm{x}})=f_{0}({\bm{x}})\mkern 1.5mu{-}\mkern 1.5mu\Theta({\bm{x}},\mathcal{X})\Theta(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{X})^{-1}f_{0}(\mathcal{X})] captures predictive uncertainty, due to the randomness of [MATH f_{0}] . Now, if we suppose that, at initialisation, [MATH f_{0}\overset{d}{\sim}\mathcal{GP}(0,k)] for an arbitrary kernel [MATH k:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{C\times C}] , then we have [MATH f_{\infty}(\cdot)\overset{d}{\sim}\mathcal{GP}(\mu({\bm{x}}),\Sigma({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime}))] for two inputs [MATH {\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime}] , where: 1 1 1 Throughout this work, the notation “ [MATH \mkern 1.5mu{+}\mkern 1.5muh.c.] ” means “plus the Hermitian conjugate”, like Lee et al. [23] . For example: [MATH \Theta^{\mathstrut}_{{\bm{x}}\mathcal{X}}\Theta_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{X}}^{-1}k^{\mathstrut}_{\mathcal{X}{\bm{x}}^{\prime}}+h.c.=\Theta^{\mathstrut}_{{\bm{x}}\mathcal{X}}\Theta_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{X}}^{-1}k^{\mathstrut}_{\mathcal{X}{\bm{x}}^{\prime}}+\Theta^{\mathstrut}_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\mathcal{X}}\Theta_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{X}}^{-1}k^{\mathstrut}_{\mathcal{X}{\bm{x}}}]

For a generic kernel [MATH k] , Lee et al. [23] observed that this limiting distribution for [MATH f_{\infty}] does not have a posterior GP interpretation unless [MATH k] and [MATH \Theta] are multiples of each other, .

As mentioned in Section 1 , previous work [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] has shown that there is a distinct but closely related kernel [MATH \mathcal{K}] , known as the Neural Network Gaussian Process (NNGP) kernel, such that [MATH f_{0}\overset{d}{\rightarrow}\mathcal{GP}(0,\mathcal{K})] at initialisation in the infinite width limit and [MATH \mathcal{K}\neq\Theta] . Thus Eq. ( 6 ) with [MATH k{=}\mathcal{K}] tells us that, for wide NNs under squared error loss, there is no Bayesian posterior interpretation to a trained NN, nor is there an interpretation to a trained deep ensemble as a Bayesian posterior predictive approximation.
3 Proposed modification to obtain posterior samples in infinite width limit

Lee et al. [23] noted that one way to obtain a posterior interpretation to [MATH f_{\infty}] is by randomly initialising [MATH f_{0}] but only training the parameters in the final linear readout layer, as the contribution to the NTK [MATH \Theta] from the parameters in final hidden layer is exactly the NNGP kernel [MATH \mathcal{K}] . 2 2 2 Up to a multiple of last layer width in standard parameterisation. [MATH f_{\infty}] is then a sample from the GP posterior with prior kernel NNGP, [MATH \mathcal{K}] , and noiseless observations in the infinite width limit i.e. [MATH f_{\infty}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime})\overset{d}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{X}^{\prime}\mathcal{X}}^{\mathstrut}\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{X}}^{-1}\mathcal{Y},\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{X}^{\prime}\mathcal{X}^{\prime}}^{\mathstrut}\mkern 1.5mu{-}\mkern 1.5mu\mathcal{K}^{\mathstrut}_{\mathcal{X}^{\prime}\mathcal{X}}\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{X}}^{-1}\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{X}^{\prime}}^{\mathstrut})] . This is an example of the “sample-then-optimise” procedure of Matthews et al. [34] , but, by only training the final layer this procedure limits the earlier layers of an NN solely to be random feature extractors.

We now introduce our modification to standard training that trains all layers of a finite width NN and obtains an exact posterior interpretation in the infinite width limit with NTK parameterisation and squared error loss. For notational purposes, let us suppose [MATH {\bm{\theta}}\mkern 1.5mu{=}\mkern 1.5mu\texttt{concat}(\{{\bm{\theta}}^{\leq L},{\bm{\theta}}^{L\mkern 1.5mu{+}\mkern 1.5mu1}\})] with [MATH {\bm{\theta}}^{\leq L}\mkern 1.5mu{\in}\mkern 1.5mu\mathbb{R}^{p{-}p_{L{+}1}}] denoting [MATH L] hidden layers, and [MATH {\bm{\theta}}^{L\mkern 1.5mu{+}\mkern 1.5mu1}\mkern 1.5mu{\in}\mkern 1.5mu\mathbb{R}^{p_{L\mkern 1.5mu{+}\mkern 1.5mu1}}] denoting final readout layer [MATH L\mkern 1.5mu{+}\mkern 1.5mu1] . Moreover, define [MATH \Theta^{\leq L}\mkern 1.5mu{=}\mkern 1.5mu\Theta-\mathcal{K}] to be the p.d. kernel corresponding to contributions to the NTK from all parameters before the final layer, and [MATH \hat{\Theta}_{t}^{\leq L}] to be the empirical counterpart depending on [MATH {\bm{\theta}}_{t}] . To motivate our modification, we reinterpret [MATH f_{t}^{\text{lin}}] in Equation 3 by splitting terms related to [MATH \mathcal{K}] and [MATH \Theta^{\leq L}] :

[MATH \displaystyle f_{t}^{\text{lin}}({\bm{x}})=\underbrace{f_{0}({\bm{x}})+\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}^{L+1}}f({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}_{0})\Delta{\bm{\theta}}^{L+1}_{t}}_{\mathcal{K}}+\underbrace{\mathbf{0}_{C}+\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}^{\leq{L}}}f({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}_{0})\Delta{\bm{\theta}}^{\leq L}_{t}}_{\Theta-\mathcal{K}}] (7)

where [MATH \mathbf{0}_{C}\mkern 1.5mu{\in}\mkern 1.5mu\mathbb{R}^{C}] is the zero vector. As seen in Equation 7 , the distribution of [MATH f_{0}^{\text{lin}}({\bm{x}}){=}f_{0}({\bm{x}})] lacks extra variance, [MATH \Theta^{\leq L}({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}})] , that accounts for contributions to the NTK [MATH \Theta] from all parameters [MATH {\bm{\theta}}^{\leq L}] before the final layer. This is precisely why no Bayesian intepretation exists for a standard trained wide NN, as in Equation 6 with [MATH k\mkern 1.5mu{=}\mkern 1.5mu\mathcal{K}] . The motivation behind our modification is now very simple: we propose to manually add in this missing variance. Our modified NNs, [MATH \tilde{f}(\cdot,{\bm{\theta}})] , will then have trained distribution:

[MATH \displaystyle\tilde{f}_{\infty}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime})\overset{d}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\Theta_{\mathcal{X}^{\prime}\mathcal{X}}^{\mathstrut}\Theta_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{X}}^{-1}\mathcal{Y},\hskip 2.84526pt\Theta_{\mathcal{X}^{\prime}\mathcal{X}^{\prime}}^{\mathstrut}\mkern 1.5mu{-}\mkern 1.5mu\Theta^{\mathstrut}_{\mathcal{X}^{\prime}\mathcal{X}}\Theta_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{X}}^{-1}\Theta_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{X}^{\prime}}^{\mathstrut})] (8)

on a test set [MATH \mathcal{X}^{\prime}] , in the infinite width limit. Note that Eq. ( 8 ) is the GP posterior using prior kernel [MATH \Theta] and noiseless observations [MATH \tilde{f}_{\infty}(\mathcal{X}){=}\mathcal{Y}] , which we will refer to as the NTKGP posterior predictive. We construct [MATH \tilde{f}] by sampling a random and untrainable function [MATH \delta(\cdot)] that is added to the standard forward pass [MATH f(\cdot,{\bm{\theta}}_{t})] , defining an augmented forward pass:
[MATH \displaystyle\tilde{f}(\cdot,{\bm{\theta}}_{t})=f(\cdot,{\bm{\theta}}_{t})+\delta(\cdot)] (9)

Given a parameter initialisation scheme [MATH \texttt{init}(\cdot)] and initial parameters [MATH {\bm{\theta}}_{0}\mkern 1.5mu{\overset{d}{\sim}}\mkern 1.5mu\texttt{init}(\cdot)] , our chosen formulation for [MATH \delta(\cdot)] is as follows: 1) sample [MATH \tilde{{\bm{\theta}}}\mkern 1.5mu{\overset{d}{\sim}}\mkern 1.5mu\texttt{init}(\cdot)] independently of [MATH {\bm{\theta}}_{0}] ; 2) denote [MATH \tilde{{\bm{\theta}}}\mkern 1.5mu{=}\mkern 1.5mu\texttt{concat}(\{\tilde{{\bm{\theta}}}^{\leq L},\tilde{{\bm{\theta}}}^{L+1}\})] ; and 3) define [MATH {{\bm{\theta}}}^{*}\mkern 1.5mu{=}\mkern 1.5mu\texttt{concat}(\{\tilde{{\bm{\theta}}}^{\leq L},\mathbf{0}_{p_{L+1}}\})] . In words, we set the parameters in the final layer of an independently sampled [MATH \tilde{{\bm{\theta}}}] to zero to obtain [MATH {\bm{\theta}}^{*}] . Now, we define:
[MATH \displaystyle\delta({\bm{x}})=\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}f({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}_{0}){\bm{\theta}}^{*}] (10)

3.1 Modelling observation noise

So far, we have used squared loss [MATH \ell(y,\tilde{f}({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}))=\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(y-\tilde{f}({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}))^{2}] for [MATH \sigma^{2}{=}1] , and seen how our NTKGP training scheme for [MATH \tilde{f}] gives a Bayesian interpretation to trained networks when we assume noiseless observations. Lemma 3 of Osband et al. [24] shows us how to draw a posterior sample for linear [MATH \tilde{f}] if we wish to model Gaussian observation noise [MATH y\overset{d}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\tilde{f}({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}),\sigma^{2})] for [MATH \sigma^{2}{>}0] : by adding i.i.d. noise to targets [MATH y^{\prime}_{n}\overset{d}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(y_{n},\sigma^{2})] and regularising [MATH \mathcal{L}({\bm{\theta}})] with a weighted [MATH L^{2}] term, either [MATH \left\lVert{\bm{\theta}}\right\rVert_{\Lambda}^{2}] or [MATH \left\lVert{\bm{\theta}}\mkern 1.5mu{-}\mkern 1.5mu{\bm{\theta}}_{0}\right\rVert_{\Lambda}^{2}] , depending on if you regularise in function space or parameter space. The weighting [MATH \Lambda] is detailed in Appendix D . These methods were introduced by Osband et al. [24] for the application of Q-learning in deep reinforcement learning, and are known as Randomised Prior parameter (RP-param) and Randomised Prior function (RP-fn) respectively. The randomised prior (RP) methods were motivated by a Bayesian linear regression approximation of the NN, but they do not take into account the difference between the NNGP and the NTK. Our NTKGP methods can be viewed as a way to fix this for both the parameter space or function space methods, which we will name NTKGP-param and NTKGP-fn respectively. Similar regularisation ideas were explored in connection to the NTK by Hu et al. [37] , when the NN function is initialised from the origin, akin to kernel ridge regression.
3.2 Comparison of predictive distributions in infinite width

Having introduced the different ensemble training methods considered in this paper: NNGP; deep ensembles; randomised prior; and NTKGP, we will now compare their predictive distributions in the infinite width limit with squared error loss. Table 1 displays these limiting distributions, [MATH f_{\infty}(\cdot)\overset{d}{\sim}\mathcal{GP}(\mu,\Sigma)] , and should be viewed as an extension to Equation (16) of Lee et al. [23] .

In order to parse Table 1 , let us denote [MATH \mu_{\text{NNGP}},\mu_{\text{DE}},\mu_{\text{RP}}] , [MATH \mu_{\text{NTKGP}}] and [MATH \Sigma_{\text{NNGP}},\Sigma_{\text{DE}},\Sigma_{\text{RP}}] , [MATH \Sigma_{\text{NTKGP}}] to be the entries in the [MATH \mu({\bm{x}})] and [MATH \Sigma({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime})] columns of Table 1 respectively, read from top to bottom. We see that [MATH \mu_{\text{DE}}({\bm{x}})=\mu_{\text{NTKGP}}({\bm{x}})] if [MATH \sigma^{2}{=}0] , and [MATH \mu_{\text{RP}}({\bm{x}})=\mu_{\text{NTKGP}}({\bm{x}})] if [MATH \sigma^{2}{>}0] . In words: the predictive mean of a trained ensemble is the same when training all layers, both with standard training and our NTKGP training. This holds because both [MATH f_{0}] and [MATH \tilde{f}_{0}] are zero mean. It is also possible to compare the predictive covariances as the following proposition, proven in Section B.2 , shows:

For [MATH \sigma^{2}{=}0] , [MATH \Sigma_{\text{NTKGP}}\succeq\Sigma_{\text{DE}}\succeq\Sigma_{\text{NNGP}}] . Similarly, for [MATH \sigma^{2}{>}0] , [MATH \Sigma_{\text{NTKGP}}\succeq\Sigma_{\text{RP}}\succeq\Sigma_{\text{NNGP}}] .

3.3 Modelling heteroscedasticity

Following Lakshminarayanan et al. [11] , if we wish to model heteroscedasticity in a univariate regression setting such that each training point, [MATH ({\bm{x}}_{n},y_{n})] , has an individual observation noise [MATH \sigma^{2}({\bm{x}}_{n})] then we use the heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL loss (up to additive constant):

[MATH \displaystyle\ell(y^{\prime}_{n},\tilde{f}({\bm{x}}_{n},{\bm{\theta}}))=\frac{(y^{\prime}_{n}-\tilde{f}({\bm{x}}_{n},{\bm{\theta}}))^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}({\bm{x}}_{n})}+\frac{\log\sigma^{2}({\bm{x}}_{n})}{2}] (12)

It is easy to see that for fixed [MATH \sigma^{2}({\bm{x}}_{n})] , our NTKGP trained baselearners will still have a Bayesian interpretation: [MATH \mathcal{Y}^{\prime}\leftarrow\Sigma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}] and [MATH \tilde{f}(\mathcal{X},{\bm{\theta}})\leftarrow\Sigma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{f}(\mathcal{X},{\bm{\theta}})] returns us to the homoscedastic case, where [MATH \Sigma\mkern 1.5mu{=}\mkern 1.5mu\text{diag}(\sigma^{2}(\mathcal{X}))\mkern 1.5mu{\in}\mkern 1.5mu\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}] . We will follow Lakshminarayanan et al. [11] and parameterise [MATH \sigma^{2}({\bm{x}})\mkern 1.5mu{=}\mkern 1.5mu\sigma^{2}_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\bm{x}})] by an extra output head of the NN, that is trainable alongside the mean function [MATH \mu_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\bm{x}})] when modelling heteroscedasticity. 5 5 5 We use the sigmoid function, instead of softplus [ 11 ] , to enforce positivity on [MATH \sigma_{{\bm{\theta}}}^{2}(\cdot)] , because our data will be standardised.
3.4 NTKGP Ensemble Algorithms

We now proceed to train an ensemble of [MATH K] NTKGP baselearners. Like previous work [ 11 , 24 ] , we independently initialise baselearners, and also use a fixed, independently sampled training set noise [MATH \bm{\epsilon}_{k}\mkern 1.5mu{\in}\mkern 1.5mu\mathbb{R}^{NC}] if modelling output noise. These implementation details are all designed to encourage diversity among baselearners, with the goal of approximating the NTKGP posterior predictive for our Bayesian deep ensembles. Appendix F details how to aggregate predictions from trained baselearners. In Algorithm 1 , we outline our NTKGP-param method: data_noise adds observation noise to targets; concat denotes a concatenation operation; and [MATH \texttt{init}(\cdot)] will be standard parameterisation initialisation in the JAX library Neural Tangents [ 38 ] unless stated otherwise. As discussed by Pearce et al. [25] , there is a choice between “anchoring”/regularising parameters towards their initialisation or an independently sampled parameter set when modelling observation noise. We anchor at initialisation as the linearised NN regime only holds local to parameter initialisation [ 23 ] , and also this reduces the memory cost of sampling parameters sets. Appendix E details our NTKGP-fn method.
3.5 Classification methodology

For classification, we follow recent works [ 23 , 39 , 40 ] which treat classification as a regression task with one-hot regression targets. In order to obtain probabilistic predictions, we temperature scale our trained ensemble predictions with cross-entropy loss on a held-out validation set, noting that Fong and Holmes [41] established a connection between marginal likelihood maximisation and cross-validation.

Because [MATH \delta(\cdot)] is untrainable in our NTKGP methods, it is important to match the scale of the NTK [MATH \Theta] to the scale of the one-hot targets in multi-class classification settings. One can do this either by introducing a scaling factor [MATH \kappa>0] such that we scale either: 1) [MATH \tilde{f}\leftarrow\frac{1}{\kappa}\tilde{f}] so that [MATH \Theta\leftarrow\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}}\Theta] , or 2) [MATH e_{c}\leftarrow\kappa e_{c}] where [MATH e_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{C}] is the one-hot vector denoting class [MATH c\leq C] . We choose option 2) for our implementation, tuning [MATH \kappa] on a small set of values chosen to match the second moments of the randomly initialised baselearners, in logit space, of each ensemble method on the training set. We found [MATH \kappa] to be an important hyperparameter that can determine a trade-off between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance: see Appendix H for further details.

5 Discussion

We built on existing work regarding the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), which showed that there is no posterior predictive interpretation to a standard deep ensemble in the infinite width limit. We introduced a simple modification to training that enables a GP posterior predictive interpretation for a wide ensemble, and showed empirically that our Bayesian deep ensembles emulate the analytic posterior predictive when it is available. In addition, we demonstrated that our Bayesian deep ensembles often outperform standard deep ensembles in out-of-distribution settings for both regression and classification tasks.

In terms of limitations, our methods may perform worse than standard deep ensembles [ 11 ] when confident predictions are not detrimental, though this can be alleviated via NTK hyperparameter tuning. Moreover, our analyses are planted in the “lazy learning” regime [ 45 , 46 ] , and we have not considered finite-width corrections to the NTK during training [ 47 , 48 , 49 ] . In spite of these limitations, the search for a Bayesian interpretation to deep ensembles [ 11 ] is of particular relevance to the Bayesian deep learning community, and we believe our contributions provide useful new insights to resolving this problem by examining the limit of infinite-width.

A natural question that emerges from our work is how to tune hyperparameters of the NTK to best capture inductive biases or prior beliefs about the data. Possible lines of enquiry include: the large-depth limit [ 50 ] , the choice of architecture [ 51 ] , and the choice of activation [ 52 ] . Finally, we would like to assess our Bayesian deep ensembles in non-supervised learning settings, such as active learning or reinforcement learning.

For an NN in the linearised regime [ 23 ] , this is related to the fact that the NTK and standard parameterisations initialise parameters differently, yet yield the same functional distribution for a randomly initialised NN. In the standard parameterisation, [MATH \lambda_{j}] will be a factor of the NN width smaller than in the NTK parameterisation, but the corresponding feature map [MATH {\bm{z}}] will be a square root factor of the NN width larger. Thus, solving Eq. ( 31 ) will lead to the same functional outputs in both parameterisations, if the NN remains in the linearised regime. However, only with our NTKGP trained baselearners [MATH \tilde{f}] do you get a posterior interpretation to the trained NN because of the difference between the NNGP and the NTK that standard training does not account for, and because the linearised regime only holds locally to the parameter initialisation.

Here, we present our ensemble algorithms for NTKGP-Lin ( Algorithm 2 ) and NTKGP-fn ( Algorithm 3 ), to complement the NTKGP-param algorithm that was presented in Section 3.4 .

In Algorithm 3 we seek to reinitialise [MATH \tilde{f}_{k}({\bm{x}},{\bm{\theta}}_{0})] from [MATH \mathcal{GP}(0,\mathcal{K})] to [MATH \mathcal{GP}(0,2\Theta)] in the infinite width limit, following the randomised prior function method of Osband et al. Appendix F Aggregating predictions from ensemble members

For completeness, we now describe how to aggregate predictions from ensemble members. Given a test point [MATH ({\bm{x}},y)] , for each baselearner NN [MATH k\leq K] , we suppose we have a probabilistic prediction [MATH p_{k}(y|{\bm{x}})] obtained from the NN output. We then treat the ensemble as a uniformly-weighted mixture model over baselearners and combine predictions as [MATH p(y|{\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}(y|{\bm{x}})] . For our Bayesian deep ensembles, we can view this aggregation as a Monte Carlo approximation of the GP posterior predictive with NTK prior.

For classification tasks, this aggregation is exactly an average of predicted probabilities. For regression tasks, the prediction is a mixture of normal distributions, and we follow Lakshminarayanan et al. [11] by approximating the ensembled prediction as a single Gaussian with matched moments. That is to say, if [MATH p_{k}(y|{\bm{x}})\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{k}({\bm{x}}),\sigma^{2}_{k}({\bm{x}}))] , then we approximate [MATH p(y|{\bm{x}})] by [MATH \mathcal{N}(\mu_{*}({\bm{x}}),\sigma_{*}^{2}({\bm{x}}))] for [MATH \mu_{*}({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k}\mu_{k}({\bm{x}})] and [MATH \sigma^{2}_{*}({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k}(\mu^{2}_{k}({\bm{x}})-\mu^{2}_{*}({\bm{x}}))+\sigma^{2}_{k}({\bm{x}})] .
Appendix G Comparison of memory and computation costs for ensemble methods

There is only a negligible training-time computational overhead for our NTKGP methods compared to other ensemble methods [ 11 , 24 ] , for a training set of fixed size (e.g. MNIST, CIFAR-10). This is because one can obtain and store our fixed additive JVPs [MATH \delta] in a single pass over the training data. For test-time constrained applications, one can employ ensemble distillation [ 56 ] for our NTKGP ensembles as one would for standard deep ensembles.

For completeness, we include in Table 2 (left) the computational cost of different ensemble methods when the modified forward pass [MATH \tilde{f}] needs to be computed on the fly for new data, though we again stress that this is not necessary for train nor test time, as described in the paragraph above. A rule of thumb for a library offering forward-mode AD, like JAX [ 35 ] , is that a JVP costs on the order of three standard forward passes in terms of FLOPs. We use forward-mode AD to compute JVPs as this is known to be more memory-efficient than reverse-mode AD for JVP computation. It is worth pointing out that our methods share the same trainable parameters as standard deep ensembles, and so do not incur any additional computational cost in the backward pass.

In terms of memory, both NTKGP and RP methods require storage of extra sets of parameters in order to compute the untrainable additive functions [MATH \delta(\cdot)] and regularise in parameter space, displayed in Table 2 (right). However, the activations of the extra forward pass in the Randomised prior function method need not be stored. And moreover, forward mode JVPs are composed alongside the primitive operations that comprise the forward pass, so the memory requirements incurred by the extra JVP are independent of the NN depth for our NTKGP methods. Note that the memory bottleneck for large NNs is most often from the need to store activations for the backward pass [ 57 ] and not from storing parameter sets, hence our NTKGP ensembles are not affected by the main memory bottleneck for large NNs, relative to standard deep ensembles.

It is worth noting that our Bayesian deep ensembles still retain the distributability of standard deep ensembles. Moreover, our computational and memory costs still scale linearly in dataset size and parameter space dimension, enabling us to work with large scale datasets like Flight Delays [ 43 ] .

Finally, in this section we only compare the costs associated to different ensemble methods. Ensembles methods are known to be computationally expensive and there has been recent interest in the community to derive new methods [ 58 , 59 ] that reduce such costs. However, at the time of writing, deep ensembles [ 11 ] are state-of-the-art for uncertainty quantification tasks [ 12 ] , and hence we believe a comparison of costs between ensemble methods is most appropriate for this work.
Appendix H Scaling for one-hot targets in classification

As discussed in Section 3.5 and repeated here for completeness: because [MATH \delta(\cdot)] is untrainable in our NTKGP methods, it is important to match the scale of the NTK [MATH \Theta] to the scale of the one-hot targets in multi-class classification settings. One can do this either by introducing a scaling factor [MATH \kappa>0] such that we scale either: 1) [MATH \tilde{f}\leftarrow\frac{1}{\kappa}\tilde{f}] and so [MATH \Theta\leftarrow\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}}\Theta] , or 2) [MATH e_{c}\leftarrow\kappa e_{c}] where [MATH e_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{C}] is the one-hot vector denoting class [MATH c\leq C] . We choose option 2) for our implementation.

To set [MATH \kappa] , for each ensemble method we calculated the mean squared values of baselearner outputs at initialisation, which we define for convenience as [MATH \zeta_{0}] , on the training set for that particular ensemble method, and tuned [MATH \kappa^{2}] (based on validation accuracy) on a small linear scale centered around [MATH C\zeta_{0}] , where [MATH C] is the number of classes. This is in order to match the second moments of the random NNs at initialisation with the scaled one-hot targets across the [MATH C] classes. For example, for NTKGP-param, we set [MATH \zeta_{0}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}|}\sum_{{\bm{x}}\in\mathcal{X}}\Theta({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}})\in\mathbb{R}^{+}] .

To illustrate the importance of [MATH \kappa] , in Figure 6 we present the corresponding results to Figure 5 where instead of setting [MATH \kappa] dependent on the scale of each ensemble methods’ initialised baselearners, as above, we set [MATH \kappa=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}|}\sum_{{\bm{x}}\in\mathcal{X}}\Theta({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}){\in}\mathbb{R}] for all ensemble methods. This is the base [MATH \kappa] value for NTKGP-param at initialisation, but note that we did not tune neither [MATH \kappa] (around this base value) nor weight variance (set at [MATH \sigma_{W}^{2}=2] like He initialisation [ 44 ] , which has been optimised for standard NNs and hence standard deep ensembles) for Figure 6 .

In Figure 6 we see a different results to Figure 5 , as here our NTKGP methods suffer slightly on in-distribution performance but also outperform the baselines methods on out-of-distribution detection. This highlights the importance of the regression target scale when considering classification tasks, and moreover reflects a general theme in our experiments of the trade-off between more aggressive predictions (that tend to perform better on in-distribution) and more conservative predictions (that tend to perform better on out-of-distribution). In our classification methodology, larger [MATH \kappa] values tend to lead to more confident predictions. We point out that this is an issue that affects all ensemble methods and is not limited to our Bayesian ensembles.
